blocks.x: Statistical Hypotheses

A statistical hypothesis is a statement about the parameters of one or more populations (or about the form of the distribution). A hypothesis test is a rule, based on a random sample, for deciding between two hypotheses:
the null hypothesis $H_0$, the claim assumed true unless the data contradict it, written as an equality such as $H_0:\mu=50$;
the alternative hypothesis $H_1$, the claim accepted if $H_0$ is rejected, such as $H_1:\mu\ne50$.

The two hypotheses are not treated symmetrically. We begin by assuming $H_0$ is true, and reject it only if the sample would be very unlikely under $H_0$. This is a proof by contradiction made probabilistic. For that reason the claim we hope to establish is placed in $H_1$.

A propellant must have a mean burning rate of $50$ cm/s. To test whether a new batch meets this we take $H_0:\mu=50$ against $H_1:\mu\ne50$. A manufacturer who wants evidence that a new process has reduced the defect rate below $5\%$ would test $H_0:p=0.05$ against $H_1:p<0.05$.
Tests of Statistical Hypotheses

A test uses a test statistic (a function of the sample) and a rejection region (critical region): the set of values of the statistic for which $H_0$ is rejected. The boundary values are the critical values.

blocks.name: Definition
blocks.title: Type I and Type II errors

blocks.x: $\alpha=\Prob(\text{Type I error})=\Prob(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ true})$ is the significance level (or size) of the test. $\beta=\Prob(\text{Type II error})=\Prob(\text{fail to reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ false})$. The power of the test is $1-\beta=\Prob(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ false})$. Note that $\beta$ depends on which specific alternative value of the parameter is true.

$\alpha$ is the false-alarm rate and $1-\beta$ is the detection rate. For a fixed sample size the two errors trade off: shrinking the rejection region lowers $\alpha$ but raises $\beta$. Only a larger sample can reduce both. Because $\alpha$ is chosen directly while $\beta$ is not, rejecting $H_0$ is a strong conclusion (error rate controlled at $\alpha$), while failing to reject is a weak one (it may be due to low power). That is why one says “fail to reject $H_0$” rather than “accept $H_0$”.

blocks.caption: Distribution of the test statistic under $H_0$ and under one alternative. The tail of the $H_0$ curve beyond the critical value is $\alpha$; the part of the $H_1$ curve to the left of it is $\beta$.

blocks.x: One-Sided and Two-Sided Hypotheses
Two-sided: $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$, $H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0$; the rejection region is in both tails.
One-sided (upper): $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$, $H_1:\mu>\mu_0$; rejection region in the upper tail.
One-sided (lower): $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$, $H_1:\mu<\mu_0$; rejection region in the lower tail.

A bottler requires a mean bursting strength of at least $200$ psi. Formulation (a): $H_0:\mu=200$ against $H_1:\mu>200$. Rejecting $H_0$ is a strong conclusion, so the manufacturer must demonstrate that the bottles exceed the specification; bottles are judged unsatisfactory unless the data prove otherwise, and there is some probability that good bottles (true mean slightly above $200$) are not accepted. Formulation (b): $H_0:\mu=200$ against $H_1:\mu<200$. Now the bottles are accepted unless there is strong evidence that they fall short, and some probability remains that bottles slightly below $200$ are judged satisfactory. Which is correct depends on the situation: (a) suits a supplier with a history of problems or safety-critical use; (b) suits a supplier with a good record where small deviations are harmless. In either case put the statement about which a strong conclusion is wanted in the alternative hypothesis.
The alternative must be chosen from the scientific question before seeing the data. Choosing a one-sided alternative after looking at which way the data lean doubles the true $\alpha$.
General Procedure for Hypothesis Testing
From the problem context, identify the parameter of interest.
State the null hypothesis $H_0$.
Specify an appropriate alternative hypothesis $H_1$.
Choose the significance level $\alpha$.
Determine an appropriate test statistic.
State the rejection region for the statistic.
Compute the sample quantities, substitute into the test statistic and find its value (and the $P$-value).
Decide whether $H_0$ should be rejected and report that in the problem context.

sections.title: Tests on the Mean of a Normal Distribution, Variance Known

blocks.x: Hypothesis Tests on the Mean
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be a random sample from $\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma^2$ known. Test $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$. If $H_0$ is true, then $\bar{X}\sim\Normal(\mu_0,\sigma^2/n)$, so
Z_0=\frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim\Normal(0,1).
For a given $\alpha$, reject $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ in favour of
$H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0$ if $\abs{z_0}>z_{\alpha/2}$;
$H_1:\mu>\mu_0$ if $z_0>z_\alpha$;
$H_1:\mu<\mu_0$ if $z_0<-z_\alpha$.
Each test has Type I error exactly $\alpha$.

The burning rate of a propellant has $\sigma=2$ cm/s. For a sample of $n=25$, $\bar{x}=51.3$. Test $H_0:\mu=50$ against $H_1:\mu\ne50$ at $\alpha=0.05$. The statistic is $z_0=(51.3-50)/(2/\sqrt{25})=3.25$. Since $\abs{3.25}>z_{0.025}=1.96$, reject $H_0$: there is evidence that the mean burning rate differs from $50$ cm/s.
$P$-Values in Hypothesis Tests
Reporting only “reject” or “fail to reject” at a fixed $\alpha$ hides how strong the evidence is.

The $P$-value is the smallest level of significance at which the observed value of the test statistic would lead to rejection of $H_0$; equivalently, the probability, computed assuming $H_0$ is true, of obtaining a test statistic value at least as extreme (in the direction of $H_1$) as the one observed.

For the $z$-test with observed $z_0$: $P=2\big[1-\Phi(\abs{z_0})\big]$ for the two-sided alternative; $P=1-\Phi(z_0)$ for $H_1:\mu>\mu_0$; $P=\Phi(z_0)$ for $H_1:\mu<\mu_0$. The rule: reject $H_0$ if $P<\alpha$.
In Example 3.8, $P=2[1-\Phi(3.25)]=2(0.00058)=0.0012$. The data would be very unusual if $\mu$ were $50$; $H_0$ would be rejected at every conventional level.

The $P$-value is not the probability that $H_0$ is true, and $1-P$ is not the probability that $H_1$ is true. It is the probability of data this extreme if $H_0$ were true. A small $P$ also does not measure the size of the effect: with a huge sample a trivial difference gives a tiny $P$ (see Section 3.2.6).
Connection Between Hypothesis Tests and Confidence Intervals

The two-sided level-$\alpha$ test of $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ rejects if and only if $\mu_0$ lies outside the $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$. The one-sided tests correspond to one-sided bounds, at the same $\alpha$:
$H_1:\mu>\mu_0$ is rejected at level $\alpha$ iff $\mu_0<\bar{x}-z_\alpha\sigma/\sqrt n$, i.e. iff $\mu_0$ lies below the $100(1-\alpha)\%$ lower confidence bound.
$H_1:\mu<\mu_0$ is rejected at level $\alpha$ iff $\mu_0>\bar{x}+z_\alpha\sigma/\sqrt n$, i.e. iff $\mu_0$ lies above the $100(1-\alpha)\%$ upper confidence bound.
$\abs{\bar{x}-\mu_0}>z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n$ is exactly the statement that $\mu_0\notin\big[\bar{x}-z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n,\ \bar{x}+z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n\big]$.
So a confidence interval answers every possible two-sided hypothesis test at once: it is the set of all values $\mu_0$ that would not be rejected.

blocks.name: Common pitfall
blocks.title: do not mix one-sided tests with two-sided intervals

blocks.x: A one-sided test at $\alpha=0.05$ uses $z_{0.05}=1.645$ and matches a one-sided $95\%$ bound. A two-sided $95\%$ interval uses $z_{0.025}=1.96$ and matches a two-sided test at $\alpha=0.05$. If a one-sided test at $\alpha=0.05$ rejects but $\mu_0$ is still inside the two-sided $95\%$ interval, there is no contradiction: the interval corresponds to the two-sided test, which has a stricter cutoff. To compare a one-sided test with an interval, use the two-sided $90\%$ interval (whose end is a one-sided $95\%$ bound) or the one-sided $95\%$ bound. The same holds for $t$, $\chi^2$ and $F$ procedures: one-sided uses $\alpha$ in a single tail, two-sided uses $\alpha/2$ in each.
Type II Error and Choice of Sample Size

Suppose the true mean is $\mu=\mu_0+\delta$ with $\delta\ne0$. Then $\bar{X}\sim\Normal(\mu_0+\delta,\sigma^2/n)$ and $Z_0=\dfrac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim\Normal\Big(\dfrac{\delta\sqrt n}\sigma,\ 1\Big)$.
For the two-sided test,
\beta=\Phi\Big(z_{\alpha/2}-\frac{\delta\sqrt n}\sigma\Big)-\Phi\Big(-z_{\alpha/2}-\frac{\delta\sqrt n}\sigma\Big).

For the one-sided alternative $H_1:\mu>\mu_0$ (with $\delta>0$), $\beta=\Phi\big(z_\alpha-\delta\sqrt n/\sigma\big)$; for $H_1:\mu<\mu_0$ ($\delta<0$), $\beta=1-\Phi\big(-z_\alpha-\delta\sqrt n/\sigma\big)$.
$\beta=\Prob(-z_{\alpha/2}\le Z_0\le z_{\alpha/2})$ with $Z_0\sim\Normal(\delta\sqrt n/\sigma,1)$; subtract the mean and use $\Phi$.

In Example 3.8 suppose the true mean is $51$, so $\delta=1$ and $\delta\sqrt n/\sigma=1\cdot5/2=2.5$. With $\alpha=0.05$, $\beta=\Phi(1.96-2.5)-\Phi(-1.96-2.5)=\Phi(-0.54)-\Phi(-4.46)=0.2946-0.0000=0.295$. The test misses a shift of $1$ cm/s about $29.5\%$ of the time; its power there is about $70.5\%$.

The properties of $\beta$: it decreases as $\abs{\delta}$ increases (large departures are easier to detect), as $n$ increases and as $\alpha$ increases, and it increases with $\sigma$. A plot of $\beta$ (or the power) against $\delta$ is the operating characteristic (OC) curve (or power curve); textbooks tabulate OC curves in terms of the standardised difference $d=\abs{\delta}/\sigma$.
To achieve Type II error $\beta$ at a specified true difference $\delta$ with a level-$\alpha$ test, use approximately
n\approx\frac{(z_{\alpha/2}+z_\beta)^2\sigma^2}{\delta^2}\quad\text{(two-sided)},\qquad n=\frac{(z_\alpha+z_\beta)^2\sigma^2}{\delta^2}\quad\text{(one-sided)}.
(The two-sided formula neglects the term $\Phi(-z_{\alpha/2}-\delta\sqrt n/\sigma)$, which is negligible when $\beta$ is small.)

For Example 3.13, how large must $n$ be to detect $\delta=1$ with probability $0.90$ ($\beta=0.10$) at $\alpha=0.05$? $n=(z_{0.025}+z_{0.10})^2\sigma^2/\delta^2=(1.96+1.28)^2(2)^2/1^2=42$. (The textbook’s operating characteristic charts with $d=\delta/\sigma=0.5$ give a very similar value, about $40$.)

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Textbook examples: propellant burning rate, continued

blocks.x: Strong versus weak conclusions. If we wish to show with a strong conclusion that the burning rate is below $50$ cm/s, we take $H_0:\mu=50$, $H_1:\mu<50$, since rejecting $H_0$ is always the strong conclusion. Failing to reject does not mean $\mu=50$ exactly, only that there is no strong evidence for $H_1$ ($H_0$ is understood to include every value not covered by $H_1$). Test. $\sigma=2$, $n=25$, $\bar{x}=51.3$: $z_0=(51.3-50)/(2/\sqrt{25})=3.25>1.96$, so $H_0:\mu=50$ is rejected at $\alpha=0.05$ (two-sided $P=2[1-\Phi(3.25)]\approx0.0012$), with strong evidence that the mean exceeds $50$. Power. If the true mean is $51$ ($\delta=1$, $d=\delta/\sigma=0.5$), with $n=25$: $\beta=\Phi(1.96-2.5)-\Phi(-1.96-2.5)\approx0.30$, i.e. about a $30\%$ chance of missing a shift of $1$ cm/s. To detect a shift of $1$ cm/s with probability $0.90$ ($\beta=0.10$) we need $n=(z_{\alpha/2}+z_\beta)^2\sigma^2/\delta^2=(1.96+1.28)^2(4)/1=42$; the OC chart gives about $40$, in close agreement. OC curves exist for the two-sided case (charts VIa, VIb) and the one-sided cases (VIc, VId); for given $n$ and $\alpha$, larger departures are detected more easily, and for a given departure a larger $n$ gives a smaller $\beta$.
Large Sample Test
If $n$ is large (say $n\ge40$), the central limit theorem justifies the $z$-test even without normality, and replacing $\sigma$ by $s$ is harmless:
Z_0=\frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt n}\ \text{ is approximately }\Normal(0,1)\text{ when }H_0\text{ is true}.
All the decision rules of Theorem 3.7 then apply.
Some Practical Comments on Hypothesis Tests

Statistical versus practical significance. A test can detect a difference too small to matter if $n$ is large, and can miss an important difference if $n$ is small. Always report the estimated size of the effect with a confidence interval, not just $P$.
$\alpha$ is chosen by the analyst, conventionally $0.05$ or $0.01$; the $P$-value lets the reader judge for themselves.
Assumptions matter. Independence and (for small $n$) normality should be checked.
Do not choose the hypotheses after looking at the data. Testing many hypotheses and reporting the significant ones inflates the false-positive rate (Chapter 13).

sections.title: Tests on the Mean of a Normal Distribution, Variance Unknown

blocks.x: Hypothesis Tests on the Mean
When $\sigma$ is unknown and the population is normal, replace $\sigma$ by $S$; the statistic then follows a $t$ distribution.
To test $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ use $T_0=\dfrac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt n}$, which has a $t_{n-1}$ distribution when $H_0$ is true. Reject $H_0$ in favour of
$H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0$ if $\abs{t_0}>t_{\alpha/2,n-1}$;

A drilled shaft is specified to have a mean diameter $2.5$ mm. A sample of $n=16$ has $\bar{x}=2.58$ and $s=0.12$. Test $H_0:\mu=2.5$ against $H_1:\mu\ne2.5$ at $\alpha=0.05$. $t_0=(2.58-2.5)/(0.12/4)=2.667$. With $15$ degrees of freedom $t_{0.025,15}=2.131$. Since $2.667>2.131$, reject $H_0$.
$P$-Value for a $t$-Test

The $P$-value is a tail area under $t_{n-1}$. Tables give only a few critical points, so the $P$-value is usually bracketed. In Example 3.18, $t_{0.01,15}=2.602$ and $t_{0.005,15}=2.947$, so the one-sided tail area is between $0.005$ and $0.01$ and the two-sided $0.01<P<0.02$ (software gives $P=0.0176$).
Choice of Sample Size

If the true mean is $\mu_0+\delta$, the statistic $T_0$ has a noncentral $t$ distribution with noncentrality $\delta\sqrt n/\sigma$, and $\beta$ must be computed from it (software, or the OC curves in terms of $d=\abs{\delta}/\sigma$). A good approximation for planning is the normal-theory formula of Theorem 3.14 plus a small correction:
n\approx\frac{(z_{\alpha/2}+z_\beta)^2\sigma^2}{\delta^2}+\frac{z_{\alpha/2}^2}2.
Since $\sigma$ is unknown, a rough estimate from a pilot study or past data is needed; the answer is only as good as that estimate.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Textbook example: golf club coefficient of restitution

blocks.x: $n=15$ drivers, $\bar{x}=0.83725$, $s=0.02456$. To show the mean exceeds $0.82$ at $\alpha=0.05$: $H_0:\mu=0.82$, $H_1:\mu>0.82$. $t_0=(0.83725-0.82)/(0.02456/\sqrt{15})=2.72>t_{0.05,14}=1.761$: reject $H_0$ ($P\approx0.008$, just under $0.01$). The normal probability plot supports normality, and since the aim is to show the mean exceeds $0.82$, a one-sided alternative is appropriate. Sample size: if the mean exceeds $0.82$ by $0.02$, then $d=0.02/0.02456=0.81$; the OC chart with $n=15$ gives $\beta\approx0.10$, so $n=15$ is adequate for power at least $0.8$.
Likelihood Ratio Approach to Development of Test Procedures (CD Only)
The tests above are all instances of one general construction.
Let $L(\theta)$ be the likelihood, $\Theta_0$ the set of parameter values allowed by $H_0$ and $\Theta$ the full parameter space. The likelihood ratio is
\Lambda=\frac{\max_{\theta\in\Theta_0}L(\theta)}{\max_{\theta\in\Theta}L(\theta)}\in[0,1],
and the test rejects $H_0$ for small values of $\Lambda$ (data much more probable under the best unrestricted parameter than under the best parameter allowed by $H_0$).

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: The $t$-test is a likelihood ratio test

blocks.x: For a normal sample, the unrestricted maximum of the likelihood uses $\hat\mu=\bar{x}$, $\hat\sigma^2=\frac1n\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2$; under $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ it uses $\hat\sigma_0^2=\frac1n\sum(x_i-\mu_0)^2=\hat\sigma^2+(\bar{x}-\mu_0)^2$. Then $\Lambda=(\hat\sigma^2/\hat\sigma_0^2)^{n/2}=\big[1+\tfrac{t_0^2}{n-1}\big]^{-n/2}$, a decreasing function of $\abs{t_0}$. Rejecting for small $\Lambda$ is the same as rejecting for large $\abs{t_0}$.

Under $H_0$ and regularity conditions, $-2\ln\Lambda$ has approximately a chi-square distribution as $n\to\infty$, with degrees of freedom equal to the number of parameters restricted by $H_0$. So reject if $-2\ln\Lambda>\chi^2_{\alpha,r}$.

sections.title: Tests on the Variance and Standard Deviation of a Normal Distribution

blocks.x: The Hypothesis Testing Procedures
Test $H_0:\sigma^2=\sigma_0^2$ for a normal population. The statistic is
\chi_0^2=\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma_0^2},\qquad\chi_0^2\sim\chi^2_{n-1}\text{ when }H_0\text{ is true.}
Reject $H_0:\sigma^2=\sigma_0^2$ in favour of
$H_1:\sigma^2\ne\sigma_0^2$ if $\chi_0^2>\chi^2_{\alpha/2,n-1}$ or $\chi_0^2<\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}$;
$H_1:\sigma^2>\sigma_0^2$ if $\chi_0^2>\chi^2_{\alpha,n-1}$;
$H_1:\sigma^2<\sigma_0^2$ if $\chi_0^2<\chi^2_{1-\alpha,n-1}$.
Tests on $\sigma$ are the same with $\sigma_0^2$ replaced by its square.

A filling machine is acceptable if $\sigma^2\le0.01$. A sample of $n=20$ has $s^2=0.0153$. Test $H_0:\sigma^2=0.01$ against $H_1:\sigma^2>0.01$ at $\alpha=0.05$. $\chi_0^2=19(0.0153)/0.01=29.07$ and $\chi^2_{0.05,19}=30.14$. Since $29.07<30.14$, do not reject $H_0$ ($P\approx0.065$): the evidence of a variance exceeding the limit is suggestive but not conclusive at the $5\%$ level.

$n=20$ bottles, $s^2=0.0153$; is the variance above $0.01$ (fluid ounces)$^2$? $H_0:\sigma^2=0.01$, $H_1:\sigma^2>0.01$, $\alpha=0.05$. $\chi_0^2=(n-1)s^2/\sigma_0^2=19(0.0153)/0.01=29.07<\chi^2_{0.05,19}=30.14$: do not reject, no strong evidence of a problem. From the table, $27.20<29.07<30.14$ gives $0.05\sigma_0^2$) or $\chi^2_{1-\alpha,n-1}$ in the lower tail (for $H_1:\sigma^2<\sigma_0^2$); two-sided uses $\chi^2_{\alpha/2,n-1}$ and $\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}$. Power: here $\sigma_0=0.10$; if the true $\sigma$ is $25\%$ larger ($\lambda=1.25$) the OC chart with $n=20$ gives $\beta\approx0.6$, so only about a $40\%$ chance of rejecting; to reach $\beta=0.20$ at $\lambda=1.25$ the chart gives $n\approx75$ bottles.
$\beta$-Error and Choice of Sample Size

If the true variance is $\sigma^2=\lambda^2\sigma_0^2$, then $(n-1)S^2/\sigma_0^2=\lambda^2V$ with $V\sim\chi^2_{n-1}$. For the two-sided test with critical values $c_L=\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}$, $c_U=\chi^2_{\alpha/2,n-1}$,
\beta=\Prob\big(c_L\le\lambda^2V\le c_U\big)=\Prob\Big(\frac{c_L}{\lambda^2}\le V\le\frac{c_U}{\lambda^2}\Big),

and for the upper one-sided test $\beta=\Prob\big(V\le\chi^2_{\alpha,n-1}/\lambda^2\big)$. OC curves in terms of $\lambda=\sigma/\sigma_0$ tabulate these. A large $\lambda$ (a big increase in the standard deviation) is detected with moderate $n$, but small departures from $\sigma_0$ need large samples.
Large-Sample Tests on a Proportion

Let $X$ be the number of successes in $n$ trials, $\hat{P}=X/n$, and test $H_0:p=p_0$. Under $H_0$, $X$ is binomial$(n,p_0)$, approximately normal with mean $np_0$ and variance $np_0(1-p_0)$ when $np_0\ge5$ and $n(1-p_0)\ge5$:
Z_0=\frac{X-np_0}{\sqrt{np_0(1-p_0)}}=\frac{\hat{P}-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}\approx\Normal(0,1).
The decision rules are those of Theorem 3.7.

A process makes $5\%$ defectives. After a change, $x=4$ defectives are found in $n=200$ items. Test $H_0:p=0.05$ against $H_1:p<0.05$ at $\alpha=0.05$. $z_0=(4-200\cdot0.05)/\sqrt{200\cdot0.05\cdot0.95}=-6/3.082=-1.947<-1.645$, so reject $H_0$ ($P=\Phi(-1.947)=0.0258$): the defect rate has been reduced.

A customer requires fraction defective at most $0.05$. To demonstrate capability the manufacturer takes $n=200$ devices and finds $4$ defective. The claim to be demonstrated goes in $H_1$: $H_0:p=0.05$, $H_1:p<0.05$, $\alpha=0.05$. $z_0=(4-200(0.05))/\sqrt{200(0.05)(0.95)}=-6/3.082=-1.95<-1.645$: reject $H_0$ ($P=0.0256$); the process is capable. Software also gives the one-sided $95\%$ upper confidence bound $0.0363<0.05$, consistent with rejection: a one-sided test goes with a one-sided bound, here an upper bound because $H_1:ptwo-sided $95\%$ interval would use $z_{0.025}=1.96$ and have a larger upper limit.) Power: if the true $p$ is $0.03$, $\beta\approx0.7$ (power only $0.3$) with $n=200$; to allow $\beta=0.10$ at $p=0.03$ with $\alpha=0.05$ the sample size needed is $n\approx832$, large because $0.05$ versus $0.03$ is a small difference.
Small-Sample Tests on a Proportion (CD Only)

When the normal approximation is poor, use the exact binomial distribution. For $H_1:p>p_0$ the $P$-value is $\Prob(X\ge x\mid p=p_0)=\sum_{k\ge x}\binom nkp_0^k(1-p_0)^{n-k}$; for $H_1:p<p_0$ it is $\Prob(X\le x\mid p=p_0)$; for a two-sided alternative one doubles the smaller tail (capped at $1$).

A machine should succeed $30\%$ of the time. If it succeeds $x=11$ times in $n=20$ trials, is its success rate higher ($H_0:p=0.3$ against $H_1:p>0.3$)? $P=\Prob(X\ge11\mid n=20,p=0.3)=0.0171$, so $H_0$ is rejected at $\alpha=0.05$.
Type II Error and Choice of Sample Size
If the true proportion is $p\ne p_0$, then $\hat{P}\approx\Normal\big(p,p(1-p)/n\big)$ and, for the two-sided test,
\beta\approx\Phi\Big(\frac{p_0-p+z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}}\Big)-\Phi\Big(\frac{p_0-p-z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}}\Big).
Solving for $n$ (two-sided, ignoring the second term; replace $z_{\alpha/2}$ by $z_\alpha$ for one-sided):
n\approx\left[\frac{z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)}+z_\beta\sqrt{p(1-p)}}{p-p_0}\right]^2.

To detect an increase of the defect rate from $p_0=0.05$ to $p=0.07$ with power $0.9$ ($\beta=0.1$) at $\alpha=0.05$ (one-sided): $n=\big[(1.645\sqrt{0.0475}+1.2816\sqrt{0.0651})/0.02\big]^2=\big[(0.3585+0.3270)/0.02\big]^2=1175$ items.

sections.title: Summary of Inference Procedures for a Single Sample

blocks.x: The table above is for two-sided alternatives. The one-sided versions, with the matching one-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ bound, are:

Reading rule: a “greater than” alternative is paired with a lower bound (the data must push the parameter above $\mu_0$, so we ask whether the lowest plausible value is still above it); a “less than” alternative is paired with an upper bound.

A goodness-of-fit test checks whether the population follows a specified distribution. Divide the range of the variable into $k$ classes (bins). Let $O_i$ be the observed frequency in class $i$ and $E_i=np_i$ the expected frequency, where $p_i$ is the probability of class $i$ under the hypothesised distribution.
Under $H_0$ (the data come from the specified distribution), the statistic

has approximately a chi-square distribution with $k-p-1$ degrees of freedom, where $p$ is the number of parameters of the distribution that were estimated from the data. Reject $H_0$ if $x_0^2>\chi^2_{\alpha,k-p-1}$. The approximation requires every $E_i\ge5$ (combine adjacent classes if necessary).

A die is rolled $60$ times, with counts $8,12,9,11,14,6$ for faces $1$ to $6$. Under $H_0$ (fair die) $E_i=10$. $x_0^2=(4+4+1+1+16+16)/10=4.2$ with $k-1=5$ degrees of freedom ($p=0$). Since $4.2<\chi^2_{0.05,5}=11.07$, we do not reject fairness.

Suppose the number of defects per unit is to be tested against a Poisson distribution whose mean is estimated by $\bar{x}$ from the same data. With $k=5$ classes after combining, $p=1$ parameter is estimated, so the degrees of freedom are $k-p-1=3$. Estimating a parameter uses up one degree of freedom because it makes the fit look better than it would for a fixed specified distribution.

Poisson. $n=60$ printed circuit boards with $32, 15, 9, 4$ boards having $0,1,2,3$ defects: the estimated mean is $\hat\lambda=(0\cdot32+1\cdot15+2\cdot9+3\cdot4)/60=0.75$. Expected counts are $60p_i$ with $p_i$ from Poisson($0.75$); the last expected count is below $3$, so the last two cells are combined, leaving $k=3$ cells, and the degrees of freedom are $k-p-1=3-1-1=1$ because one parameter was estimated. $\chi_0^2=2.94<\chi^2_{0.05,1}=3.84$: cannot reject the Poisson model ($P=0.0864$). Minimum expected frequencies of $3$, $4$ or $5$ are widely used; cells with smaller expected counts are combined with neighbours and $k$ is reduced. Normal, equiprobable cells. For $n=100$ power-supply voltages ($\bar{x}=5.04$, $s=0.08$) choose $k=8$ cells with equal probability $0.125$, so every expected count is $np_i=12.5$; for the standard normal the boundaries are $0,\ \pm0.32,\ \pm0.675,\ \pm1.15$ (times $s$, plus $\bar{x}$). Two parameters are estimated, so the degrees of freedom are $8-2-1=5$; the test statistic is $0.64$, against $\chi^2_{0.05,5}=11.07$ (the textbook compares with $11.07$): not rejected ($P=0.9861$).

Two classifications of the same units can be summarised in an $r\times c$ contingency table, where $O_{ij}$ is the number of units in row category $i$ and column category $j$. We ask whether the two classifications are independent.
Let $R_i$ be the row totals, $C_j$ the column totals and $n$ the grand total. Under $H_0$: “the row and column classifications are independent”, the expected counts are $E_{ij}=\dfrac{R_iC_j}n$, and
Reject $H_0$ if $x_0^2>\chi^2_{\alpha,(r-1)(c-1)}$ (again requiring $E_{ij}\ge5$ roughly).

blocks.name: Proof
blocks.title: Why the degrees of freedom are $(r-1)(c-1)$

blocks.x: There are $rc$ cells. The row and column probabilities $p_{i\cdot}$ and $p_{\cdot j}$ must be estimated from the data; there are $(r-1)+(c-1)$ free estimates (each set sums to $1$). The degrees of freedom are $rc-1-[(r-1)+(c-1)]=(r-1)(c-1)$.

Two treatments are compared: treatment A has $40$ successes and $10$ failures, treatment B has $30$ successes and $20$ failures. The row totals are $50,50$, column totals $70,30$ and $n=100$. The expected counts are $35,15,35,15$. $x_0^2=\dfrac{25}{35}+\dfrac{25}{15}+\dfrac{25}{35}+\dfrac{25}{15}=4.76$ with $1$ degree of freedom. Since $4.76>\chi^2_{0.05,1}=3.84$, reject independence ($P=0.029$): the success rate depends on the treatment.

The same test applies when the data are a set of random samples from $r$ populations classified into $c$ categories (a test of homogeneity): $H_0$ is that all populations have the same category probabilities, and the statistic and degrees of freedom are identical.

Counts, never percentages, go into $O_i$ and $E_i$. The statistic is always upper-tailed (large values indicate poor fit). Small expected counts invalidate the approximation. Degrees of freedom are $k-1$ minus the number of estimated parameters for goodness of fit and $(r-1)(c-1)$ for independence. A significant result shows association, not causation, and says nothing about its strength: use a measure such as Cram'er’s $V=\sqrt{x_0^2/(n\min(r-1,c-1))}$.

$H_0$ is assumed true until the data contradict it; $\alpha=\Prob(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_0)$, $\beta=\Prob(\text{fail to reject}\mid H_0\text{ false})$, power $=1-\beta$. Rejecting is strong; failing to reject is weak.

Follow the eight steps. The $P$-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme if $H_0$ were true; reject if $P<\alpha$. A two-sided test rejects iff the value $\mu_0$ falls outside the $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval.

$z$-test (known $\sigma$): $\beta=\Phi(z_{\alpha/2}-\delta\sqrt n/\sigma)-\Phi(-z_{\alpha/2}-\delta\sqrt n/\sigma)$, $n\approx(z_{\alpha/2}+z_\beta)^2\sigma^2/\delta^2$. $t$-test: $t_0=(\bar{x}-\mu_0)/(s/\sqrt n)\sim t_{n-1}$.
Variance: $\chi_0^2=(n-1)s^2/\sigma_0^2\sim\chi^2_{n-1}$. Proportion: $z_0=(x-np_0)/\sqrt{np_0(1-p_0)}$, exact binomial for small $n$.
Likelihood ratio tests generate the standard tests; $-2\ln\Lambda\approx\chi^2$ (Wilks).
Goodness of fit: $\sum(O-E)^2/E\sim\chi^2_{k-p-1}$; independence in an $r\times c$ table: $\chi^2_{(r-1)(c-1)}$ with $E_{ij}=R_iC_j/n$.

The mean breaking strength of a cable is claimed to be at least $1800$ lb. A sample of $50$ cables has $\bar{x}=1792$ with $\sigma=15$ known. Test the claim at $\alpha=0.01$ with the eight-step procedure and find the $P$-value.
For the test in Exercise 1, compute $\beta$ when the true mean is $1785$ and the sample size needed for $\beta=0.05$ at that alternative.

Twelve measurements of the octane rating of a gasoline have $\bar{x}=88.3$ and $s=0.9$. Test $H_0:\mu=87.5$ against $H_1:\mu\ne87.5$ at $\alpha=0.05$ and compare your decision with the $95\%$ confidence interval.
Explain why the sentence “the probability that the null hypothesis is true is $0.03$” is not a correct reading of $P=0.03$. Give a correct reading.
A sample of $n=25$ has $s^2=18.5$. Test $H_0:\sigma^2=12$ against $H_1:\sigma^2>12$ at $\alpha=0.05$ and compute $\beta$ when the true variance is $24$.
In a poll of $n=500$, $265$ favour a proposal. Test $H_0:p=0.5$ against $H_1:p>0.5$ at $\alpha=0.05$. How large a sample would detect $p=0.55$ with power $0.8$?

The numbers of accidents per week over $50$ weeks are: $0$: 17 weeks, $1$: 19, $2$: 9, $3$: 4, $4$ or more: 1. Test whether a Poisson distribution with $\lambda$ estimated from the data fits ($\alpha=0.05$; combine classes as needed).

A survey cross-classifies $200$ employees by shift (day/night) and quality rating (high/medium/low): day: $50,\ 30,\ 20$; night: $20,\ 35,\ 45$. Test independence at $\alpha=0.05$ and describe the association.
